entities.summary:
The Antonine Wall, a defensive fortification built by the Romans in the 2nd century AD, marked the northernmost boundary of the Roman Empire in Britain. Constructed between 142 and 144 AD, it stretched for approximately 63 Roman miles (about 60 km or 37 miles) across the Central Lowlands of Scotland. This massive undertaking, engineered by the Roman governor Aulus Plautius, aimed to prevent Celtic incursions and secure the Roman province of Britain.

The wall, constructed using local stone and turf, was up to 12 feet (3.6 meters) wide and 10 feet (3 meters) high. It was fortified with military bases, watchtowers, and fortlets, and was an engineering marvel of its time. The wall played a crucial role in the Roman occupation of Britain, which lasted until the early 5th century AD.

The legacy of the Antonine Wall can be seen in the many archaeological discoveries and excavations that have taken place along its route. Today, the wall is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a testament to the ingenuity and engineering prowess of the ancient Romans.

As the Roman historian Tacitus wrote, 'The Antonine Wall was a bulwark against the barbarian hordes, a safeguard for the province of Britain.'
